keyVerseText: For yet seven days, and I will cause it to rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights; and every living substance that I have made will I destroy from off the face of the earth. destroy: Heb. blot out
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun יְקוּם (yᵉqûwm) derives from the root קוּם (qûwm), which carries a rich semantic field including concepts of standing, rising, enduring, and establishing. This root sense of 'to stand' or 'to remain' informs יְקוּם as referring to that which exists in a stable, enduring way—essentially, a living substance or entity that stands or subsists. Thus, beyond the English gloss of 'substance' or 'existence,' the root emphasizes the active, ongoing presence and standing of life within creation.
usageInScripture: The word יְקוּם occurs three times in Scripture, consistently conveying the idea of living substance or that which subsists. It is translated variously as 'living substance,' 'and every living substance,' and 'and all the substance,' reflecting a focus on the totality of living beings or entities that stand in existence. This consistency in usage underscores the term's role in describing the fullness of life or existence that God has created and over which He exercises sovereign authority.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding יְקוּם as 'living substance' rooted in the idea of standing or enduring enriches our grasp of God's creative and sustaining power. It reminds believers that all life is not accidental but established and maintained by God's decree. This term highlights the reality that every living thing is a standing testimony to God's ongoing creative work and His sovereign control over existence. For the Christian faith, it points to the Creator's authority over life and death and the dependability of His sustaining grace in all creation.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 7:4, God declares that He will cause rain to fall and destroy 'every living substance' (יְקוּם) He has made from the face of the earth. Here, יְקוּם emphasizes the totality of living beings subject to God's judgment during the Flood. The word conveys not just life in a general sense but the standing existence of all creatures, underscoring God's sovereign power to sustain or to remove life according to His righteous will.
